questions.q: In Trace 1 (bit-flip code, logical |1>_L = |111>, X error on qubit 2), what is the state immediately after the error, and what syndrome does it produce?
options: State 101, syndrome (Z1Z2, Z2Z3) = (1,1)
State 111, syndrome (0,0)
State 100, syndrome (1,0)
State 110, syndrome (0,1)
questions.explain: Flipping the middle bit of 111 gives 101; comparing qubit1 vs qubit2 (1 vs 0) disagrees, and qubit2 vs qubit3 (0 vs 1) disagrees, giving syndrome (1,1).

questions.q: Why does the syndrome in Trace 1 match the lesson 10 table's entry for an error on qubit 2, even though Trace 1 starts from logical |1>_L instead of |0>_L?
options: It's a coincidence; the tables for |0>_L and |1>_L are unrelated
Logical |1>_L always produces a different syndrome table than |0>_L
The syndrome depends only on where the error occurred, never on which logical state (alpha/beta) was encoded
The syndrome in this case is actually wrong and doesn't match
questions.explain: Stabilizer measurements are designed to be blind to the logical state and sensitive only to the error -- exactly why the same syndrome-to-correction mapping works regardless of which logical state was encoded.

questions.q: In Trace 2 (phase-flip code, logical |0>_L = |+++>, Z error on qubit 3), what correction does the syndrome (0,1) indicate?
options: Apply X to qubit 3
No correction needed
Apply Z to qubit 1
Apply Z to qubit 3
questions.explain: Per the lesson 11 verified table, syndrome (X1X2,X2X3)=(0,1) uniquely corresponds to an error on qubit 3, corrected by applying Z to that qubit.

questions.q: What is the common 6-step shape both traces in this lab follow?
options: Encode -> decohere -> measure -> discard -> re-encode -> repeat
Prepare ancilla -> clone data qubit -> measure clone -> compare to original -> correct -> discard
State the error -> compute each stabilizer's outcome -> assemble the syndrome -> look up the correction -> apply it -> verify
Apply Hadamard -> measure -> renormalize -> apply Hadamard again -> measure -> done
questions.explain: Both traces follow the identical procedure: identify the error, compute stabilizer outcomes directly from the physical bits, assemble the syndrome, look up and apply the correction, then verify the result.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this 6-step trace procedure matters beyond just the two 3-qubit codes?
options: The identical procedure generalizes unchanged to every stabilizer code in the course, including the Steane code and the surface code, just with more stabilizers and larger syndromes
This procedure stops working once more than one stabilizer generator is involved
It only applies to codes with exactly 3 physical qubits
Larger codes like the surface code use a fundamentally different, unrelated correction procedure
questions.explain: The same error -> syndrome -> lookup -> correct pipeline scales directly to the Steane code's 6 stabilizers and the surface code's many stabilizers, which is exactly why mastering it here pays off later.
